title: Present Tense (Polite)
plainEnglish: The everyday polite present tense — what is happening now or is generally true.
whenToUse: Reach for V-아/어요 in almost every ordinary spoken situation: an action happening right now (지금 비가 와요 — it's raining now), a daily habit (저는 매일 운동해요 — I exercise every day), and a general truth (물은 100도에서 끓어요 — water boils at 100 degrees). Korean has no separate present-continuous form, so this one ending covers both English 'I eat' and 'I am eating'; context and adverbs like 지금 (now) or 매일 (every day) tell you which. It is the friendly-polite '요-level' (해요체) you use with strangers, shopkeepers, coworkers, and older friends — polite enough to be safe, casual enough to be warm. Switch UP to the deferential -ㅂ니다/습니다 for formal announcements, the news, or a job interview (감사합니다, not 감사해요); switch DOWN to 반말 (drop 요: 먹어, 가) only with close friends, children, or people clearly younger. When unsure, 아/어요 is the default that rarely offends.
attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요 (좋다→좋아요). Otherwise add 어요 (먹다→먹어요, 읽다→읽어요). 하다 verbs become 해요 (공부하다→공부해요). Watch contractions: 가다→가요, 오다→와요, 마시다→마셔요, 주다→줘요, 보내다→보내요.
contrastWith: Confused most often with two neighbors. (1) PAST tense -았/었어요: the very same vowel rule builds both, so the only difference is the extra ㅆ — present 먹어요 'I eat' vs past 먹었어요 'I ate'; present 가요 'I go' vs past 갔어요 'I went'. Master the present and the past is nearly free. (2) FORMAL -ㅂ니다/습니다: both are polite, but -ㅂ니다 is stiffer and more public — 어디 가요? sounds like a friendly 'Where are you off to?', while 어디 갑니까? sounds like a formal interview question. Mixing them in one breath (해요 then 합니다) sounds untrained, so pick one register and hold it. Don't confuse 아/어요 with bare 반말 either: 반말 is simply this form minus 요 (먹어, 가), which flips it from polite to intimate.

examples.note: Simplest form: 마시다 contracts 시+어 → 셔, giving 마셔요 — never 마시어요. Object marked with 을.

examples.en: My older brother is listening to music now.
examples.note: Same ending = present continuous here; the adverb 지금 (now) is what makes it 'is listening'. 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ→ㄹ before 어 (들어요).

examples.ko: 죄송한데요, 지하철역이 어디예요? 그쪽으로 어떻게 가요?
examples.en: Excuse me, where's the subway station? How do I get there?
examples.note: Real street register: 가요? as a polite question to a stranger sounds natural and warm, where the formal 갑니까? would feel oddly stiff.

commonMistakes: Picking the wrong vowel: saying 먹아요 instead of 먹어요. The stem 먹- ends in ㅓ (not ㅏ/ㅗ), so it must take 어요. Only bright vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (좋아요, 봐요) take 아요.
Failing to contract: saying 가아요 for 가다 or 마시어요 for 마시다. When the stem already ends in ㅏ, the 아 merges (가요); 시 + 어 fuses to 셔 (마셔요). Korean smooths these out automatically.
Using 아/어요 in a formal setting where -ㅂ니다 is expected — e.g. opening a presentation with 안녕하세요, 발표 시작해요 instead of 시작하겠습니다 / 시작합니다. 아/어요 is correct Korean but too casual for the podium.
studyOrder: Drop 다 to find the stem
Check the last stem vowel: ㅏ/ㅗ takes 아요, everything else takes 어요
Apply 하다 → 해요 and watch for contractions (가요, 와요, 마셔요)
beginnerExplanation: The 아/어요 ending is the workhorse of Korean — the polite, everyday present tense you will use more than any other form, and the one and only form for both 'I eat' and 'I am eating'. Here's the mnemonic: think of ㅏ and ㅗ as the two 'bright, smiley' vowels (their extra stroke points up and out, like a happy face), and they like to keep the family together by pairing with 아요 — 좋다 → 좋아요, 보다 → 봐요. Every other vowel is 'dark' and pairs with 어요 — 먹다 → 먹어요, 읽다 → 읽어요. The one rebel is 하다, which always becomes 해요 (memorize 공부해요, 사랑해요, 일해요 as a set). And whenever two same-ish vowels bump into each other they fuse so your mouth doesn't repeat itself — 가다 becomes 가요, not 가아요. Lock in 아/어요 first and you'll sound natural in nearly any polite conversation; the past tense (-았/었어요) is then just this form with a tiny ㅆ added.
